questions.q: Which equation represents the lattice formation enthalpy (lattice energy) of magnesium chloride?
questions.solution: Lattice formation enthalpy is the enthalpy change when one mole of an ionic solid is formed from its gaseous ions. The equation from the elements is the enthalpy of formation, and the reverse equation is lattice dissociation. (Using aqueous ions confuses the lattice with the reverse of dissolving.)

questions.q: Which equation represents the first electron affinity of oxygen?
questions.solution: First electron affinity: one mole of gaseous atoms each gains one electron to form one mole of gaseous 1− ions. Starting from \(\mathrm{\tfrac{1}{2}O_{2}}\) would include atomisation; adding a second electron is the second electron affinity. (Starting from the element in its standard state is the common slip.)

questions.q: Use the data to calculate the lattice formation enthalpy of potassium bromide. Values in \(\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\): enthalpy of formation of KBr −394; atomisation of potassium +89; first ionisation energy of potassium +419; atomisation of bromine +112; first electron affinity of bromine −325.
questions.solution: Going round the cycle: \(\Delta_{\text{f}}H = (89 + 419 + 112 - 325) + \Delta_{\text{LE}}H\), so \(\Delta_{\text{LE}}H = -394 - 295 = -689\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}\). (Using +325 for the electron affinity leads to −1339.)

questions.q: Use the data to calculate the second electron affinity of oxygen. Values in \(\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\): enthalpy of formation of CaO −635; atomisation of calcium +178; first and second ionisation energies of calcium +590 and +1145; atomisation of oxygen +249; first electron affinity of oxygen −141; lattice formation enthalpy of CaO −3459.
questions.solution: \(\Delta_{\text{f}}H = 178 + 590 + 1145 + 249 - 141 + \text{EA}_{2} - 3459\). The known terms add up to −1438, so \(\text{EA}_{2} = -635 + 1438 = +803\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}\). It is endothermic because the electron is added to a negative ion, which repels it. (Leaving out the second ionisation energy of calcium leads to −342.)

questions.q: Which compound has the most exothermic lattice formation enthalpy?
questions.solution: Lattice enthalpy is more exothermic for ions with higher charges and smaller radii. MgO and CaO both have 2+ and 2− ions, far more strongly attracted than the 1+ and 1− ions in NaCl and KBr, and \(\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}\) is smaller than \(\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}\). (Choosing CaO overlooks the smaller magnesium ion.)

questions.q: For silver chloride, the lattice formation enthalpy from a Born–Haber cycle is \(-905\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}\), but the value calculated from the perfect ionic model is \(-833\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}\). Which statement best explains the difference?

options.A: The silver ion polarises the chloride ion, so the bonding has some covalent character, which strengthens the lattice beyond the purely ionic value.
options.B: The ions in silver chloride are larger than the perfect ionic model assumes, so they attract each other less.
options.C: The perfect ionic model leaves out the electron affinity of chlorine.
options.D: Silver chloride is perfectly ionic; the difference is experimental error.

questions.solution: The perfect ionic model treats the ions as point charges, perfectly spherical. A Born–Haber value that is more exothermic than the model shows extra bonding the model leaves out: the small silver ion distorts the large chloride electron cloud, giving partial covalent character. (A difference of about 70 kJ per mole is far too large to be experimental error.)

questions.q: Which compound would you expect to show the greatest degree of covalent character?
questions.solution: Covalent character is greatest when a small, highly charged cation (high polarising power) is paired with a large anion that is easily polarised. \(\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}\) is smaller and more highly charged than \(\mathrm{Na^{+}}\), and \(\mathrm{I^{-}}\) is much larger than \(\mathrm{F^{-}}\). (Choosing \(\mathrm{MgF_{2}}\) uses the right cation but the least polarisable anion.)

questions.q: Which equation represents the enthalpy change of hydration of the chloride ion?
questions.solution: Enthalpy of hydration: one mole of gaseous ions dissolves in water to form one mole of aqueous ions. Dissolving the whole solid is the enthalpy of solution. (Writing the reverse, from aqueous to gaseous ions, is the common slip.)

questions.q: Calculate the enthalpy change of solution of calcium chloride. Values in \(\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\): lattice dissociation enthalpy of \(\mathrm{CaCl_{2}}\) +2258; enthalpy of hydration of \(\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}\) −1579; enthalpy of hydration of \(\mathrm{Cl^{-}}\) −364.
questions.solution: \(\Delta_{\text{sol}}H = \Delta H_{\text{lattice dissociation}} + \sum \Delta_{\text{hyd}}H = 2258 + (-1579) + 2(-364) = -49\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}\). (Counting only one chloride ion leads to +315.)

questions.q: Which ion has the most exothermic enthalpy change of hydration?
questions.solution: Hydration is most exothermic for small, highly charged ions, which attract the polar water molecules most strongly. \(\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}\) has a 2+ charge and is smaller than \(\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}\). (Choosing \(\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}\) matches the charge but not the smaller radius.)

questions.q: For which reaction is the entropy change of the system negative?
questions.solution: Four moles of gas become two moles of gas in the ammonia synthesis: fewer ways to arrange the particles, so the system's entropy falls. Each of the other reactions produces gas from a solid or a liquid, so its entropy rises. (Thinking that forming a compound always increases entropy is the slip.)

questions.q: Calculate the entropy change for \(\mathrm{N_{2}(g) + 3H_{2}(g) \rightarrow 2NH_{3}(g)}\). Standard entropies in \(\text{J K}^{-1}\ \text{mol}^{-1}\): \(\mathrm{N_{2}}\) 192; \(\mathrm{H_{2}}\) 131; \(\mathrm{NH_{3}}\) 193.
questions.solution: \(\Delta S = \sum S(\text{products}) - \sum S(\text{reactants}) = 2(193) - [192 + 3(131)] = 386 - 585 = -199\ \text{J K}^{-1}\ \text{mol}^{-1}\). (Ignoring the coefficients in the equation leads to −130.)

questions.q: For the synthesis of ammonia, \(\Delta H = -92\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}\) and \(\Delta S = -199\ \text{J K}^{-1}\ \text{mol}^{-1}\). What is \(\Delta G\) at 298 K?
questions.solution: Convert \(\Delta S\) to kJ: \(-0.199\ \text{kJ K}^{-1}\ \text{mol}^{-1}\). Then \(\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S = -92 - 298 \times (-0.199) = -92 + 59.3 = -32.7\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}\). (Leaving \(\Delta S\) in J leads to \(+5.9 \times 10^{4}\).)

questions.q: For \(\mathrm{CaCO_{3}(s) \rightarrow CaO(s) + CO_{2}(g)}\), \(\Delta H = +178\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}\) and \(\Delta S = +161\ \text{J K}^{-1}\ \text{mol}^{-1}\). Above what temperature does the decomposition become feasible?
questions.solution: It becomes feasible when \(\Delta G = 0\), so \(T = \frac{\Delta H}{\Delta S} = \frac{178000}{161} = 1106\ \text{K}\). (Not converting kJ to J leads to 1.11 K.)

questions.q: The graph shows how \(\Delta G\) for a reaction varies with temperature. What are \(\Delta H\) and \(\Delta S\) for the reaction?

figure.alt: Free-energy change against temperature: a straight line that starts at +120 kJ per mol at 0 K, falls steadily, crosses zero at 800 K and reaches −30 kJ per mol at 1000 K.

questions.solution: \(\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S\) is a straight line with intercept \(\Delta H\) and gradient \(-\Delta S\). Intercept: \(\Delta H = +120\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}\). Gradient \(= \frac{0 - 120}{800} = -0.150\ \text{kJ K}^{-1}\ \text{mol}^{-1}\), so \(\Delta S = +150\ \text{J K}^{-1}\ \text{mol}^{-1}\). (Taking the gradient itself as \(\Delta S\) leads to −150.)

questions.q: At 298 K, \(\Delta G\) for the conversion of diamond to graphite is negative. Which statement best explains why diamonds do not turn into graphite?

options.A: The entropy change is negative, so the change is not feasible.
options.B: The change is endothermic, so it needs a continuous supply of heat.
options.C: A negative \(\Delta G\) means the change is feasible only at high pressure.
options.D: The activation energy is very high, so the rate at room temperature is negligible.

questions.solution: A negative \(\Delta G\) means the change is thermodynamically feasible, but says nothing about its rate. Turning diamond into graphite means breaking strong C–C bonds, so the activation energy is enormous: the change is kinetically inhibited. (Concluding the change is not feasible contradicts the negative \(\Delta G\).)

questions.q: For the synthesis of ammonia at 298 K, \(\Delta H = -92\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}\) and \(\Delta S_{\text{system}} = -199\ \text{J K}^{-1}\ \text{mol}^{-1}\). What is \(\Delta S_{\text{total}}\)?
questions.solution: \(\Delta S_{\text{surroundings}} = -\frac{\Delta H}{T} = -\frac{-92000}{298} = +309\ \text{J K}^{-1}\ \text{mol}^{-1}\). Then \(\Delta S_{\text{total}} = -199 + 309 = +110\ \text{J K}^{-1}\ \text{mol}^{-1}\), so the reaction is feasible at 298 K. (Getting the sign of \(\Delta S_{\text{surroundings}}\) wrong leads to −508.)

questions.q: For a reaction at 298 K, \(\Delta G = -11.4\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}\). Use \(\Delta G = -RT\ln K\) to find the equilibrium constant, \(K\). (\(R = 8.31\ \text{J K}^{-1}\ \text{mol}^{-1}\))
questions.solution: \(\ln K = -\frac{\Delta G}{RT} = \frac{11400}{8.31 \times 298} = 4.60\), so \(K = \mathrm{e}^{4.60} = 99.8\). A negative \(\Delta G\) goes with \(K > 1\). (Stopping at \(\ln K\) leads to 4.60.)

questions.q: A reaction has a positive \(\Delta H\) and a positive \(\Delta S\). Which statement is correct?

options.A: It becomes feasible above a certain temperature.
options.B: It is feasible at all temperatures.
options.C: It is not feasible at any temperature.
options.D: It is feasible only below a certain temperature.

questions.solution: In \(\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S\), the positive \(\Delta H\) works against feasibility, but \(-T\Delta S\) is negative and grows with temperature. Above \(T = \frac{\Delta H}{\Delta S}\), \(\Delta G\) becomes negative. (Feasible only at low temperature is the case for negative \(\Delta H\) and negative \(\Delta S\).)

questions.q: Ammonium nitrate dissolves in water spontaneously at room temperature, even though its enthalpy change of solution is positive. Which statement best explains this?

options.A: The entropy of the surroundings increases because the solution becomes colder.
options.B: The entropy of the system rises so much, as the lattice breaks up into freely moving aqueous ions, that the total entropy change is positive.
options.C: The hydration enthalpies are more exothermic than the lattice dissociation enthalpy is endothermic.
options.D: Dissolving does not change the entropy of the system, so only the enthalpy change matters.

questions.solution: The endothermic change takes heat from the surroundings, so \(\Delta S_{\text{surroundings}}\) is negative. Breaking an ordered lattice into mobile ions gives a large positive \(\Delta S_{\text{system}}\), which outweighs it: \(\Delta S_{\text{total}}\) is positive, so \(\Delta G\) is negative. (If the hydration enthalpies outweighed the lattice enthalpy, \(\Delta_{\text{sol}}H\) would be negative, not positive.)
